env_override.note: an integer string, the shape a workflow sets
set but empty — a shell expanding an unset var
a unit suffix, which float() will not take
zero is not 'no ceiling', it is a typo

expect.note: five things: `over_budget` says 70.00s is inside the ceiling and 70.01s is not; `fast` is the only key in WALL_BUDGET_S, checked as a set; EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S moves the ceiling for a positive number and falls back to the committed 70 for everything else; `evals.run.main()` returns 1 on an over-budget total and 0 otherwise; and .github/workflows/eval.yml declares the CI ceiling this case pins

provenance: the `fast` gate's wall clock went 13s (M2) -> 48.6s (M6) -> 55.4s (M7) -> 67.5s (M8) without one run ever turning red, because ADR-002 Decision 4's 60s ceiling was prose in an ADR and nothing read it. This case has been falsified three times, each one level up from the last, and carries a half for each. (1) It first read `sorted(evals/report/*-fast.json)[-1]`; on the fresh clone `.github/workflows/eval.yml` builds, the newest file is always the report the branch committed, so a tree measuring 77.23s still scored 89/89 = 1.000 with the gate green (PR #20 R1). (2) It then graded `evals.run.over_budget` alone, and the five-line block in `main()` that applies it was pinned by nothing: deleting `evals/run.py`'s `if over_budget(args.suite, totals["wall_seconds"]):` left a 79.02s run — 32% over — reporting 90/90 = 1.000 at exit 0 with this case PASSing (PR #20 R8). Watched red with that block deleted and nothing else touched: `[FAIL] fast-wall-clock-budget`, 89/90 = 0.989 against baseline 1.000, wrong: [{wall_seconds: 79.02, exit: 1, got: 0}] — failing on the run that should have been stopped and not on the one that should not. (3) The ceiling then met CI for the first time and turned out never to have run there: main's own CI does `fast` in 89.62s, ~50% over the same 60s, invisibly. The ceiling became per-environment (ADR-013 Decision 3), so the override is now part of the ruling. Both directions watched red before it existed: with `wall_budget` ignoring the environment, the two positive-value rows fail (`{'env': '95', 'expected_ceiling': 95.0, 'got': 60}`); with an unguarded `float()` that lets garbage mean 'no ceiling', six rows fail (`{'env': None, 'expected_ceiling': 60, 'got': inf}`). The workflow row was red before `.github/workflows/eval.yml` declared anything: `{'workflow': 'EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S', 'declared': None, 'expected': 75}`.

triage.note: grades a rule and the place it is applied, because holes have appeared at both. `_main_exit_code` drives the real `evals.run.main()` with `load_cases`/`run_case` stubbed to a single result of a chosen duration — no case runs, no report is written, stdout and stderr are swallowed — so what is graded is the value `main()` RETURNS. One line short of the path CI takes: `evals/run.py`'s `if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())` tail is what turns that value into a process exit code, `_main_exit_code` calls `main()` in-process and never goes through it, and changing the tail to a bare `main()` would disable this ceiling — and the invariant and regression rules with it — with this case still green (PR #20 R13, Debt T-R13). The suite-key check is a set comparison rather than a row per suite name: rows can only ever cover the suites someone thought to list, and `full` was the one missing when `WALL_BUDGET_S["full"] = 1` was shown to slip through green (PR #20 R11). The env-override rows are all fallback except two, for the same reason: the dangerous direction is an override that quietly switches the gate off, not one that fails to apply.
triage.not_covered: it grades total wall clock only — a case that gets 10s slower while another gets 10s faster is invisible to it; per-case timings are in every committed report for anyone looking. It does not drive `evals/run.py` as a process, so the module tail described above is ungraded. It does not exercise the `--update-baseline` path, which returns before the ceiling is consulted and reports nothing about it (PR #20 R12, Debt T-R12). Slower hardware is answered rather than uncovered: `EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S` gives an environment its own measured ceiling, and this case grades the override's fallbacks and the value the workflow declares — but nothing here checks that a declared number was ever measured. This case cannot tell a measured 75 from an invented one; only an ADR-013 amendment with runs behind it can.
